title: Computing Shear Viscosities from Molecular Dynamics Simulation: Comparing the OrthoBoXY Approach with the Green-Kubo Method
authors: Marcel Brandt, Ralf Ludwig, Dietmar Paschek
abstract: We calculated shear viscosities of 15 neat molecular liquids from equilibrium molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using the OrthoBoXY approach and compare them to viscosities calculated via the Green-Kubo method. Data from both methods agree very well. Here, we show how to avoid pitfalls while computing the OrthoBoXY-data to obtain optimal results. From simulations of multiple system sizes, we could verify that the viscosity of molecular liquids is not influenced by finite size effects down to systems as small as 250 molecules. Moreover, we demonstrate that also the standard error of the viscosity is nearly independent of the system size. This is shown to be a consequence of a compensation effect of an increasing accuracy of the self-diffusion coefficients with increasing systems-size and the system-size dependent weighting according to the OrthoBoXY-equation. As a consequence, we suggest that it is preferable to run simulations of smaller systems with longer simulation times rather than larger systems with shorter simulation runs. In addition, we discuss a refinement of the recently introduced "recipe" for OrthoBoXY simulations block-lengths $τ_\mathrm{block}$. Based on data from simulations with varying run-lengths, we suggest the following modification: for highly viscous systems, the value of $τ_\mathrm{block}$ might safely be scaled by a factor of $1/8$, significantly reducing the computational resources needed. For less viscous systems, the value of $τ_\mathrm{block}$ might safely be scaled by a factor of $1/4$. For systems with high fluidity, the value of $τ_\mathrm{block}$ should not be scaled down in order to achieve reliable results. When using a smaller system size of 250 molecules, these refinements are leading up to a 24-fold reduction in computational cost compared to the previous recommended set-up without sacrificing numerical accuracy.
summary: This work compares two methods for calculating liquid shear viscosity from MD simulations, confirming strong agreement between them. The authors demonstrate that the results are robust against finite size effects and propose practical guidelines for scaling simulation parameters ($\tau_{\text{block}}$) to achieve massive computational savings without losing numerical accuracy.
main_problem: The paper addresses the accurate computation of shear viscosities ($\eta$) for molecular liquids using Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, comparing two established theoretical approaches.
main_result: Both the OrthoBoXY and Green-Kubo methods yield highly consistent results across a wide range of liquid viscosities. Furthermore, the study provides significant computational recommendations to reduce simulation time without sacrificing accuracy.
method: The viscosity is calculated using MD simulations in the NVT ensemble, comparing the stress tensor autocorrelation function (Green-Kubo) against an approach derived from self-diffusion coefficients (OrthoBoXY).
model_or_system: The study investigates 15 neat molecular liquids modeled using the OPLS force field. The analysis covers systems ranging across three orders of magnitude in viscosity.
key_observables: Shear viscosity ($\eta$), self-diffusion coefficients ($D_0$, $D_{PBC,ii}$), and their associated standard errors.
important_parameters: System size (down to 250 molecules), simulation block length ($	au_{	ext{block}}$), and temperature/density conditions for the liquids.
main_assumptions: The OrthoBoXY approach relies on a specific geometric relationship involving box lengths, and statistical robustness is achieved by using Variant C averaging method.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the agreement between different viscosity calculation methods (OrthoBoXY vs. Green-Kubo) and show how error estimates are independent of system size due to compensation effects.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the problem and compares the two main computational methods. It then analyzes the dependence on system size, confirming robustness down to small systems. Finally, it proposes detailed, quantitative refinements for setting the simulation block length ($	au_{	ext{block}}$) based on liquid viscosity.
why_interesting: While focused on classical liquids, the rigorous statistical analysis of error propagation and the development of scaling rules (like adjusting $\tau_{\text{block}}$ by $1/8$ or $1/4$) are highly relevant to optimizing resource-intensive simulations in quantum many-body systems.
